extracted.intended_audience: USPTO rulemakers, patent practitioners, patent owners, and patent policy stakeholders
extracted.subtask_short: comment on USPTO terminal disclaimer rule
extracted.subtask_description: A formal organizational comment responding to the USPTO's proposed rule on terminal disclaimer practice to obviate nonstatutory double patenting, arguing legal, procedural, policy, and practical objections and recommending withdrawal of the proposed rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory constraint on USPTO rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO’s authority derives from statutes enacted by Congress and the Administrative Procedure Act (APA); important limitations include the inability to (i) establish regulations inconsistent with statutes; and (ii) undertake substantive rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed rule exceeds USPTO authority because it is inconsistent with 35 U.S.C. §§ 253(a), 282(a), and 288 and constitutes substantive rulemaking beyond what Congress has legislated. See Merck & Co. v. Kessler and Tafas v. Doll for limits on substantive rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-by-claim validity principle (35 U.S.C. § 253(a), § 282(a), § 288)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 253(a) states that '[w]henever a claim of a patent is invalid the remaining claims shall not thereby be rendered invalid.' This requirement also appears in 35 U.S.C. §§ 282(a) and 288.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any practice or rule must preserve the statutory principle that validity and enforceability are determined on a claim-by-claim basis; a rule that eliminates claim-by-claim analysis and renders all claims unenforceable because a single claim is invalid contradicts these statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on rendering unrelated claims unenforceable
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule would render all claims of a patent unenforceable as a result of the invalidity of any claim in another patent encompassed by a terminal disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulemaking should not allow an invalidity determination for one claim to preclude enforceability of another claim that is not patentably indistinct; doing so is inconsistent with statutes and relevant Federal Circuit decisions (e.g., Ortho Pharm. Corp. v. Smith).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of procedural rulemaking—substantive effect test
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule that dramatically impacts continuation practice and the enforceability of patent holders’ rights constitutes substantive rulemaking, which the USPTO lacks authority to promulgate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a rule effectively restricts applicants’ statutory rights (e.g., ability to file continuations under 35 U.S.C. § 120 or to enjoy full patent scope), it is substantive. Tafas v. Doll is cited as precedent where the Federal Circuit rejected USPTO limits on continuations as substantive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers and enforcement prerogatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent enforcement is within the purview of the courts; the USPTO may examine and grant patents but should not create new post-issuance enforcement limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO should not impose requirements that intrude on judicial enforcement authority (35 U.S.C. §§ 271–299). Creating post-issuance unenforceability consequences via administrative rulemaking is inconsistent with separation of powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process protection for patent property rights (Fifth Amendment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are property (35 U.S.C. § 261); depriving a patent owner of enforceability without appropriate procedural and evidentiary safeguards raises Fifth Amendment due process concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules that would require surrender or stripping of property-like patent rights (or produce equivalent effects) without Article III-type safeguards are constitutionally suspect; historical precedent (McCormick Harvesting) cautions against requiring surrender absent statutory authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of retroactive application and protection of reliance interests
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule is ambiguous about retroactive effect on issued patents and pending applications; retroactive application could affect already-issued patents and settled reliance interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulemaking should avoid retroactive effects that disrupt settled expectations, interfere with investments, or affect patents filed years before implementation; clarity on non-retroactivity is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to facilitate and expedite processing (35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(C))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 2(b)(2)(C) requires the USPTO to establish regulations that 'shall facilitate and expedite the processing of patent applications.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A new rule that discourages filing terminal disclaimers, induces petitions, prolongs prosecution, or otherwise increases processing time fails this statutory mandate. The USPTO must assess whether the rule will impede rather than facilitate and expedite processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating incentives for gamesmanship and shifting adjudication to examiners
rubrics_metrics.description: Linking enforceability of multiple patents via terminal disclaimers creates an incentive for challengers to target a single claim to potentially render an entire family unenforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy should avoid shifting validity/enforceability adjudication from Article III courts (and PTAB processes) to examiners without evidentiary hearings, which risks inconsistent and less robust evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy should not increase prosecution complexity or costs
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule will complicate patent examination and increase the cost of obtaining meaningful patent protection, for example by inducing omnibus filings, more restriction appeals, and litigation to avoid terminal disclaimers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulemaking should consider and avoid predictable behavioral responses that increase applicant costs and examiner burdens, and disproportionately affect small entities and universities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of practitioners’ ethical duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule overlooks the ethical duties of loyalty and diligent representation that patent attorneys and agents owe clients, which may compel practitioners to refrain from recommending or signing terminal disclaimers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO should account for how rule changes might create implicit ethical obligations for practitioners (e.g., to avoid terminal disclaimers) that extend prosecution time and expense; rules should not indirectly force such conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of small businesses and promotion of competition
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule may disproportionately harm small businesses, which have limited resources to pursue expensive prosecution strategies, potentially discouraging technology transfer and harming competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulemakers should assess distributive impacts and avoid policies that unduly burden small entities or reduce incentives for innovation and investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with Federal Circuit precedent on continuation and terminal disclaimer practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule is inconsistent with Federal Circuit cases (e.g., In re Cellect, Ortho Pharm.) and judicially developed doctrines related to continuation practice and terminal disclaimers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO regulations should be consistent with controlling case law and cannot create requirements unsupported by appellate decisions; the rule conflicts with cases recognizing independent enforceability of terminally disclaimed patents and guidance on filing terminal disclaimers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve continuation practice under 35 U.S.C. § 120
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuation practice allows applicants to pursue claims of different wording, scope, and variation and is essential to define claim scope; continuations are entitled to the parent's priority date subject to § 120 limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations should not undermine the statutory continuation mechanism, should respect written description/enabling requirements (35 U.S.C. § 112, M.P.E.P. § 201.07), nor improperly restrict applicants’ ability to file continuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use evidence-based analysis for policy about drug patents and continuations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions that continuation practice causes delayed generic entry or excessive patent thickets (as in some I-MAK claims) are empirically disputable; USPTO study data contradict sensational claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy decisions should rely on rigorous evidence (e.g., USPTO Drug Patent and Exclusivity Study) and avoid adopting rules based on flawed datasets or anecdotal counts of patents associated with products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rulemaking premised on unsupported litigation-cost claims
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no demonstrated correlation that a greater number of continuations (or patents) necessarily increases litigation costs for generics or biosimilars; only asserted claims need be addressed in litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory action should not be justified by unfounded assumptions about litigation volume or cost increases; consider actual assertion patterns (e.g., small fraction of claims typically asserted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect incentives to correct defects via reexamination and reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule may discourage patent owners from using reexamination or reissue procedures to correct defects because fixing a claim in one patent could render the entire family unenforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations should preserve incentives and ability to correct issued patents without imposing penalties that deter use of available post-issuance corrective mechanisms.
